sections.title: From ODEs to PDEs: The Leap in Complexity
sections.content: Define Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs) as functions of a single variable (e.g., time). Introduce PDEs as equations involving functions of multiple variables (space and time), focusing on how variables 'interact' in a multi-dimensional field.
sections.example: Visualizing a ball thrown in the air (ODE) vs. the ripples on a pond caused by a stone (PDE).

sections.title: Core Concept: The Heat Equation
sections.content: Introduce the heat equation as a fundamental PDE. Use a 2D color-gradient grid to show how temperature diffuses over time. Explain that the rate of change in time equals the curvature (Laplacian) in space.
sections.example: A cat sleeping on a metal plate; show the heat map spreading from the cat's body across the plate surface over 60 seconds.

sections.title: Boundary and Initial Conditions: The 'Rules of the Game'
sections.content: Explain that PDEs alone are insufficient; they need constraints. Use an animation of a vibrating guitar string fixed at both ends to illustrate Dirichlet boundary conditions (the fixed endpoints).
sections.example: A robotic arm welding a seam; the PDE describes the heat, but the 'boundary conditions' are the physical edges of the metal sheet being welded.

sections.title: The Big Picture: Why We Solve Them
sections.content: Summarize that PDEs represent the language of nature (physics, fluid dynamics, electromagnetics). Conclude with a visual montage: weather forecasting, airplane wing design, and signal processing.
sections.example: The flow of air over a bird's wing as it glides—PDEs allow us to simulate the lift and drag forces without building every single prototype.
